newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign banks in Shanghai begin yuan business.
newsitem.headline: Foreign banks in Shanghai begin yuan business.

text.p: Two foreign banks in Shanghai on Thursday opened for local Chinese currency business for the first time since the communist takeover in 1949, a significant step in the opening up of the Chinese economy, bankers said.

One of the first Chinese yuan accounts was opened by the British Consul-General to Shanghai, Warren Townend, who deposited an auspicious 888.88 yuan ($107) in a cheque account with the Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp.
Eight is considered a lucky number in China.
The Shanghai branch of the Industrial Bank of Japan said it signed pre-agreements with two Japanese firms, Hitachi and Matsushita to take in yuan deposits.
And the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's deputy general manager in Shanghai, Tsotomu Hiroe, said his bank would also begin yuan business by the end of March.

But bankers said the scale of the business to be conducted would be very small in the initial stages, and it would probably take years before foreign banks could establish a significant presence in China's huge banking system.

"This is an historic moment not only in the history of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp in China, but also in the financial reform of China," said Eddie Wang, the bank's chief executive officer for China.

"The relaxation for foreign banks to operate renminbi (yuan) business is indeed a bold move, but more importantly reflects the confidence and determination of the country to achieve further success in reforming its banking sector," he added.
Bankers said it was significant for China and for foreign banks to have the local currency banking market opened up, even to such a small extent.
They said it would also be of some benefit in promoting China's application to join the World Trade organisation (WTO).

Only eight foreign bank branches in Shanghai have so far received permission to conduct yuan business, and they can basically only accept deposits from foreign-funded firms or from foreign individuals in Shanghai.
The banks can supply yuan loans only to foreign-funded firms or Chinese enterprises that have previously obtained foreign currency loans from the banks.
"Finally, foreign banks have made another stride forward," said a European banker. "Now it's in place, they can't revoke it and they'll have to open more."

"The foreign banks will make up only a miniscule amount of the total lending volume in China, but eventually it will grow," the banker said. "It won't have any impact on total loan volume in the coming years."
The rate at which foreign banks will be taxed for the yuan business they conduct has not yet been fixed, but several senior bankers in Shanghai said they expected it to be 33 percent.
The bankers noted that regulations governing the business were still skeletal and needed more clarification and detail.
"It will require some time," said one foreign banker. "The central bank doesn't fully understand it yet themselves. This is very much an experiment for them."
If the experiment is viewed by the central bank as a success, another banker said he saw the possibility of foreign bank branches in other cities being able to start yuan business operations in 1998.
"But there's a threat to the (Chinese) state banks in the long run, hence the restrictions," the banker said.
"The Chinese government is clever as always, satisfying some of the basic demands of foreign banks, but making sure the dominant market share of the Chinese banks is not threatened."
